articles.title: Steinmeier in China: A major state visit in uncertain times
articles.summary: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is traveling to China on a state visit in a period of political and economic uncertainty. Germany is seeking alternative partners in the region, but also wants good…

image.caption: Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to China on MondayImage: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Eight years have passed since Frank-Walter Steinmeier's last trip to China. Since then, the relationship between China and Europe has changed significantly. The German president plans to spend several days touring China before concluding his visit in Beijing, where he will meet with China's leaders.
His visit comes just as the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee is convening for its plenary session, a major annual event that foreign dignitaries usually avoid when timing their visits.

The focus of the president's five-day trip will be "Germany's diverse and complex relations with China, as well as the challenges involved," his office said in a statement. In addition to sites of cultural exchange, the itinerary will also include a visit to a Volkswagen plant in Hefei.
A diplomatic balancing act

The automotive industry, in particular, illustrates the dilemma facing Germany's China policy. China is one of the most important markets for German automotive and machinery manufacturers, as well as for the chemical industry. At the same time, state-supported overcapacity in China is putting pressure on European manufacturers.
Not only that, Germany and Europe are dependent on China for raw materials and technologies, which means they are increasingly seeking out alternative partnerships.

Steinmeier was once an advocate of the policy of "change through trade" — the idea that other countires could be persuaded to become more democratic with the leverage of global trade, now considered something of a failure.

Now he must now pursue a tougher European line in Beijing. Caught between partnership and competition, Europe leaders recently managed to reach an agreement: Imports of plug-in hybrid vehicles from China are to be scaled back.
"That was a concrete step, but it can only be the beginning," said Michael Laha, an expert on China at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) in Berlin.
Why big automakers are losing China
Chancellor and president both in Asia

Coinciding with Steinmeier's state visit to China, Chancellor Friedrich Merz is traveling to the Indo-Pacific with business representatives. His visit to Japan, Singapore, and South Korea will focus on competitiveness, technological upheavals, defense cooperation, and critical raw materials. Merz is visiting companies and attending important regional economic conferences in Tokyo and Seoul.

The dual trips are Berlin's attempt to send a twofold message: While the chancellor is "deliberately strengthening Germany's partnerships in the Indo-Pacific at a time of global upheaval," says Laha, the president is seeking dialogue with Beijing at a time when Germany and Europe are recalibrating their relationship with China.

"This joint trip sends a very well-coordinated message to the Chinese that we remain committed to the partnership but at the same time are taking steps to reduce risk," said Laha, before adding that this is a difficult balancing act that also allows China to save face.

blocks.caption: Steinmeier and Merz are traveling to Asia at the same timeImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Little room for human rights

While Merz will be accompanied by a large economic delegation, Steinmeier will be traveling to China with representatives from German culture, politics, and academia. Mikko Huotari, director of the China Institute MERICS, is also expected to be part of the delegation — even though Beijing has imposed sanctions on the institute. "The fact that he is coming along sends a clear message to the Chinese side that we do not approve of the sanctions," said Laha.

In 2021, the EU imposed sanctions against several Chinese party and regional officials, as well as an organization accused of serious human rights violations and oppressing the Uyghur minority. It was the first time such sanctions had been imposed on China since the Tiananmen Square massacre in 1989, and Beijing did not take kindly to them: In response, the Chinese government imposed entry bans and other sanctions against European politicians, scholars, and institutions, including MERICS.

Laha does not expect human rights to play a major role in the German president's trip. Steinmeier is considered a pragmatist when it comes to China policy. As foreign minister, he distanced himself from his predecessor Joschka Fischer, a critic of China, and even criticized Chancellor Angela Merkel when she hosted the Dalai Lama.

blocks.caption: China's Xi Jinping is seeking greater influence in international affairsImage: Florence Lo/Reuters/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: China should assume international responsibility

On the subject of Ukraine, Steinmeier is likely to be more direct and raise the issue of China's role in the conflict. "Beijing is clearly on Moscow's side," said Laha. In Berlin, however, officials are convinced that China can do more to persuade Russia to engage in serious negotiations and find a solution to the conflict.

Steinmeier may make this clear in his speech at Peking University on Thursday. Germany has "long viewed China's emergence with respect and goodwill," reads a statement from the president's office. Today, however, the focus is less on China's continued rise and more on how it uses its growing power.

"If the president points out that Russia used its power to attack a sovereign state, he could be alluding to another regional connection: Taiwan," says Laha. That could be seen as an appeal to Beijing to assume more responsibility for the regional and international order.

To conclude his visit, Steinmeier will meet with China's leadership in Beijing. Talks are planned with President Xi Jinping, whom he has known for nearly two decades, as well as with Premier Li Qiang and the chairman of the National People's Congress, Zhao Leji.

The trip marks the culmination of Steinmeier's focus on Asia during his second term in office. Since then, he has deliberately sought to forge close ties with partners in the region and has advocated for greater diversification. Now China – the most important and most challenging partner – will come to its own conclusion.

articles.title: Japan gives passport to 90-year-old PH-born woman separated from dad after WWII
articles.summary: The Embassy of Japan has issued a Japanese passport to Adelaida Kakazu, a 90-year-old Japanese descendant who remained in the Philippines after World War II.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 9:06pm
The Embassy of Japan has issued a Japanese passport to Adelaida Kakazu, a 90-year-old Japanese descendant who remained in the Philippines after World War II.

"Despite the hardships experienced by Japanese descendants during and after the war, Ms. Kakazu has maintained her ties with Japan. The Embassy has supported her registration in the Japanese family registry through interviews and examination of relevant documents," the Japanese Embassy said in a statement.

According to The Japan Times, Kakazu is a second-generation Japanese woman born in the Philippines. She is a Nikkei-jin, a Japanese term meaning Japanese emigrants who left Japan to live in other countries and their descendants.

She was separated from her Japanese father after World War II when the latter was repatriated. She plans to use her new passport to visit her father's native Okinawa and hopefully meet members of her family.
The embassy urged descendants wanting to acquire Japanese nationality to contact its office via this link.
It added that individual interviews for Japanese nationality acquisition will be conducted in various regions across the Philippines.
Japanese descendants are advised to prepare as many of following documents to confirm their identities:

articles.title: LemFi launches ‘Ambition has no passport,’ its biggest product expansion yet
articles.summary: An expanded platform for people living and moving across borders? Meet LemFi's newest milestone

blocks.text: An expanded platform for people living and moving across borders? Meet LemFi's newest milestone

items: LemFi launches the biggest product expansion in its history, adding UK savings, credit, and data eSIM in 100+ destinations.
This rebuilt app brings transfers, savings, credit and connectivity together in one platform for people building financial lives across borders.
New global brand "Ambition has no passport" reflects LemFi’s evolution from remittances into a broader financial platform serving more than two million customers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by LemFi and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

LemFi, the financial platform for people building lives across borders, announced the launch of its new global brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, alongside a completely rebuilt app, launching the largest product expansion in its history.

More than two million customers use LemFi to move money to more than 30 countries, with over $2 billion in monthly transaction volume, and the company plans to add more countries next year. The expanded platform now includes savings and credit in the UK, eSIMs in more than 100 destinations, alongside LemFi’s existing international payments service.

People who move countries arrive with a career, a qualification and a savings record, only to find that almost none of it counts. A credit history rarely survives a border crossing. Around 304 million people now live outside the country where they were born, sending some $905 billion home each year. However, many financial services remain designed around individual products or customers living their financial lives in a single country. LemFi is building its platform around that gap, extending from the international transfers on which the company was founded into a wider range of financial services designed for people whose lives span borders.

“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned is that the harder problem starts after the transfer,” said Ridwan Olalere, co-founder and CEO of LemFi. “Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time. That is the wrong answer for people this ambitious, so we have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do. Ambition travels. The infrastructure behind it should travel too.”

blocks.caption: LemFi co-founder and CEO Ridwan Olalere and co-founder and CFO Rian Cochran

blocks.text: Transfers, still at the heart of it. Send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond, from the same account that now saves, borrows and connects.

Savings that stay within reach in the UK. The LemFi Instant Access Savings Account currently pays a boosted 5% AER for the first six months from account opening; it then reverts to 3.04% AER (tracker), tracking the Bank of England base rate. Accounts open from £1, with no penalty for withdrawals. Deposits are held by ClearBank and protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to £120,000 per eligible depositor.

A credit history that travels in the UK. A revolving credit line, available subject to availability, is issued by Lemfi Credit through Pillar, the FCA-regulated credit provider LemFi acquired in 2025. It is available as a virtual card through Apple Pay and Google Pay and can be used for both spending and sending. Eligible customers can also see their Equifax credit score in the app for free.
eSIM in more than 100 destinations, in every market. Buy mobile data before arriving, with no SIM swap and no roaming bill.

The app has been re-architected from the ground up to hold several products across several countries in a single account, rather than bolting them onto a transfer app. The redesign also brings LemFi’s products to the forefront of the experience, making them easier to discover and creating an architecture that lets the company add new services as it expands.

The company has also introduced its new global brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, reflecting its focus on customers building careers, businesses, families and financial lives across borders. The new identity spans LemFi’s product interface, website, marketing and social channels and will roll out across its global markets.

“LemFi started as a way to send money home. Our customers turned it into a way to build a life across borders,” said Isabel Ron-Pedrique, vice president of design and brand at LemFi. “They are not defined by the country they left. They are defined by what they are building. Ambition has no passport is not a line we placed on top of the product. It is the idea the whole system is built from, from the app you open in the morning to the poster you walk past on the way to work. We have built this brand to keep up with them.”
Savings and credit are available in the UK at launch, with other markets to follow. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Molbog leader raises fears, concerns over Balabac EDCA site
articles.summary: Molbog people, still awaiting certifications of their claim to ancestral lands, protest the developments on Balabac Island

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Molbog indigenous people Emmanuel San Esteban and Anjilon Flores during a presser in Quezon City on Monday, October 26.
Molbog people, still awaiting certifications of their claim to ancestral lands, protest the developments on Balabac Island

items: A Molbog indigenous leader expressed concerns over the construction of military facilities on Balabac Island, which disrupts their ancestral land and daily lives.
The construction includes a three-kilometer runway, and the indigenous community is protesting the developments, citing loss of sacred sites and intimidation from unknown individuals.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A Molbog indigenous leader raised fears and concerns over disruptions to their ancestral land and daily lives caused by the construction of military facilities on Balabac Island in southern Palawan.

Balabac Island faces the West Philippine Sea and sits between the Sulu Sea and the South China Sea (connected by the Balabac Strait). It is designated as one of the four additional sites under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

As Balabac is becoming what defense experts say is one of the most consequential military hotspots, indigenous people are protesting the developments on the land they claim as ancestral domain. Among the constructions on the island is a three-kilometer runway.

“‘Yung libingan ng aming ninuno, tinambakan (The graveyard where we bury our ancestors, they filled with soil),” Emmanuel San Esteban, president of indigenous-led group Bangsa Molbog, said during a briefing in Quezon City on Monday, October 26.

“At ‘yung bundok na pinagri-ritwalan noon ay wala na po. Tinibag na rin.” (And the mountain where we hold our rituals before is gone. It was cleared.) The Molbog leader also said he experienced physical harm and intimidation from unknown men.
Last May, US, Australian, and Philippine Army soldiers conducted a live-fire assault on the island as part of the Balikatan exercises.
San Esteban said their people were taken aback by the military drills conducted earlier this year.

“Hindi namin po alam na magpapaputok pala sila doon sa sinasabing EDCA,” said San Esteban. “[‘Yung] mga tao, nagtakbuhan, lalo na po [ang] mga kabataan.” (We didn’t know they would open fire in the EDCA site. The people fled, especially the young ones.)

He was accompanied by Anjilon Flores, also of the Molbog people, who expressed concerns about livelihood and the government’s National Greening Program (NGP). Flores, who spoke in the Molbog language translated by San Esteban, said the state’s program restricted them from farming and their access to food. Some lands where they used to farm are now covered by the reforestation program.

The Molbog people have been applying for their certificate of ancestral domain — an area spanning 26,000 hectares in Catagupan village on Balabac Island. Balabac, composed predominantly of Molbog people, has a population of 42,662. Catagupan, San Esteban’s village and the site of the runway, has a population of a little over 2,000 people.
Earlier in October, human rights group Karapatan denounced alleged military and police harassment of journalists and researchers in Balabac.

Karapatan said “the incident has brought even more fear to the local Molbog community, which has been suffering intimidation and the destruction of the environment in their ancestral lands due to the construction of the EDCA site.”
Rappler has reached out to the Armed Forces of the Philippines Western Command for comment, but it has yet to respond as of posting. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’
articles.summary: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand

blocks.text: Electric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers.
Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.
The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and then sell some of it back to the grid at times of high demand.

If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it could help to solve one of the big problems of the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.

The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteries can do the same job.

Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need to pay renewable generators to switch off.
However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.

Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known as bidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets.

The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could mean an additional 147m tonnes of carbon emitted into the atmosphere by 2050.

Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, a thinktank tracking the transition to electric cars, said: “Vehicle to grid is exciting technology that could help balance the grid and cut bills, but carmakers should only be rewarded if it’s actually used, not just for fitting it.

“Under these proposals, one or even two extra credits worth around £4,000 each would hand manufacturers thousands per car for kit that costs a few hundred pounds, even though few drivers own the expensive charger needed to use it. Ministers should make sure the people who benefit from V2G are drivers and billpayers, not carmakers’ shareholders.”
after newsletter promotion

Some people already sell their electricity back to the grid through companies such as Octopus Energy in the UK, Renault in France, and BMW in Germany. Octopus Energy has claimed that drivers could save £620 a year with the service.

Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Association England, which represents drivers, said: “We have millions of EV drivers in the UK, but only a fraction are using vehicle to grid or storage technologies. These technologies have enormous potential but consumers are still getting to grips with more immediate questions around the cost of their car, the cost of charging, and whether an EV meets their day to day needs.

“It is far too early to be giving manufacturers a credit that effectively allows them to sell fewer EVs, for a technology that has not even been tried and tested, at scale, by drivers in the real world.”

Once the technology takes off, electricity supplied by V2G cars could add up to the equivalent of a power station by 2030, able to provide 1.2 gigawatts of power on demand, according to the National Energy System Operator, which balances Great Britain’s grid. That could grow to as much as 41 GW by 2050, Neso forecasts, enough to meet more than a quarter of peak energy demand.

articles.title: Prenup won't dispute VP Sara and husband's undeclared assets, says Ridon
articles.summary: A prenup between Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio won"t change the fact that the couple had over P800 million worth of undeclared assets, Rep. Terry Ridon said.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 8:54pm

A pre-nuptial agreement between Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio won’t change the fact that the couple had over P800 million worth of undeclared assets, House prosecutor Terry Ridon of Bicol party-list said Monday.

Ridon made the response when asked of the take put forward by private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan in a separate television interview that the defense might bring up a prenup between Duterte and Carpio to disassociate the Vice President from her husband's assets.
Ridon said that the spouses filed a joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth and jointly filed income taxes.

“It is an observation of one of our private prosecutors and that fact should still be put in place during the defense’s presentation of evidence. But irrespective of whether it is absolute community property, conjugal property or separation of property, the SALN law does not make distinctions. Kailangan pa rin po ilagay iyong pag-aari ng mag asawa,” Ridon said in a press conference.
(The SALN law requires spouses to declare all their assets.)
“And in fact, in each and every document… the tax document or the SALN document, joint ho iyong filing nila. So, antayin natin kung papaano nila ilalapag ito pong defense na ito,” he added.
(They have joint filing of SALN and tax records, so we'll see how they defend this.)
Ridon said that in 2023 alone, the Duterte couple had P100 million in their bank deposits, compared to their declared joint net worth of P80 million.

“More than P100 million in bank deposits, investments and insurance had not been stated in the SALN of the Vice President. Just for that matter, they would have to explain why is such discrepancy,” he said.
Ridon speculated that Duterte will declare her ignorance when the defense starts its presentation of evidence on November 9.

“I think ‘yung magiging defense po doon ay hindi niya po alam ‘yun pong lahat po ng mga financial transactions, una ng kanyang ama at ng kanya pong asawa. But again, I don’t think that is a defense,” Ridon said.
(I would think her defense is that she would not know the financial transactions of her husband and father.)

The House prosecution panel dropped three of the four impeachment charges against Duterte—Article 1, alleging misuse of confidential funds; Article 3, bribery; and Article 4, grave threats against President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr.—after lawyer and certified public accountant Alex Cabrera testified on Duterte's alleged unexplained wealth.

Cabrera concluded that Duterte and Carpio had unexplained wealth amounting to P817 million to P1.5 billion, after reviewing the couple's financial records including SALNs, bank transaction and bank deposit records, insurance payment records, income tax returns and corporate records of their business interests.

As a result, the impeachment case against the Vice President rests only on Article 2, which alleges unexplained wealth due to non-declaration of assets in the SALN and non-divestment of businesses despite a Constitutional prohibition.

Lawyer Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) also identified P4.4 billion in aggregate covered and suspicious transactions involving Duterte and Carpio from 2007 to 2025. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman
articles.summary:
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa

Prosecutors in

blocks.text: Prosecutors in Japan have filed formal charges against a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.

Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcaster NHK reported.

Ballard had initially been arrested in Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.

NHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.

Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station when he was arrested, Japanese media reported.

Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban for US military members stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.
Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.
A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.
US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.
There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.

After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

articles.title: Sara Duterte's husband Mans Carpio is complainant in cyberlibel case, says Lustre lawyer
articles.summary: The lawyer of journalist Philip Lustre Jr., who was arrested over the weekend for a cyberlibel complaint, said that Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, was the complainant in the…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 8:36pm

The lawyer of journalist Philip Lustre Jr., who was arrested over the weekend for a cyberlibel complaint, said that Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, Manases Carpio, was the complainant in the case, as shown by a document filed with the Davao City Regional Trial Court.

“Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases “Mans” Carpio, is behind the online libel complaint that led to the arrest of 72-year-old journalist Philip Lustre Jr,” said Atty. Dino De Leon in a statement on Monday.

De Leon said that according to a copy of the information his law firm obtained from the Davao court, Lustre was accused of posting statements on Facebook imputing a crime to Carpio on or about March 6, 2026.

“That on or about March 6, 2026, in the City of Davao, and within the jurisdiction of this Honorable Court, the above-named accused, with deliberate intent, willfully, unlawfully, and feloniously, through his Facebook account, under the name ‘Philip Jr Lustre,' published and posted written statements, thereby making an imputation of a crime against Atty. Masanes R. Carpio, a private individual and on the said date, was actually residing in Davao City, through the internet using the social networking platform called Facebook.com,” a portion of the Information read.

blocks.caption: (From the FB post of Atty. Dino De Leon)

blocks.text: (From the FB post of Atty. Dino De Leon)

Lustre was arrested by police officers in Quezon City on Saturday morning based on an arrest warrant for cyberlibel issued by a Davao court. He said he was unaware of any complaint lodged against him.
The 72-year-old journalist is the author of the book Kill, Kill, Kill, which is about the Duterte administration's war on drugs, and is a longtime critic of the Dutertes.

Sought for their side, Carpio's camp said, "The lawyers of Atty. Maneses Carpio are carefully reviewing the latest developments. We will provide an update as soon as an official reaction statement is available."
‘Unlawful, illegal arrest’
Lustre’s camp likewise described his arrest as “unlawful and irregular,” saying it “came like a thief in the night.”
De Leon said Lustre had no prior knowledge of the case before his arrest, adding that the address indicated on the warrant was not the journalist’s actual residence.
He questioned whether notices during the preliminary investigation had also been sent to that wrong address, thereby depriving Lustre of the opportunity to respond to the complaint.
“If it was easy for the authorities to find Philip Lustre in a media forum, why is it that they were not able to use a proper address during the preliminary investigation stage?” De Leon said.

According to De Leon, arresting officers were also unable to identify the complainant or explain the factual allegations during the arrest because the electronic warrant system displayed only the warrant itself.
He underscored the timing of the service of the warrant, noting that it was executed at a time when obtaining court documents and posting bail are more difficult.
Lustre’s arrest took place following a Saturday forum, a move De Leon argued could intimidate other members of the media.
“Make no mistake, I think this is an attack on the freedom of media and free press,” De Leon said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Chris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London club
articles.summary:
R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023

The R&B singer Chris Brown has been given a suspended sentence after…

blocks.text: The R&B singer Chris Brown has been given a suspended sentence after striking a man twice in the head with a tequila bottle in a central London club.
Brown, 37, admitted affray earlier this year after attacking a former friend with a “heavy” tequila bottle on the dancefloor at the Tape private members’ club in Mayfair in February 2023.

Brown was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, at Southwark crown court on Monday. His vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and both men were ordered to pay £1,500 costs.
In front of a packed public gallery, the singer sat looking at the floor in the dock for much of the hearing.
Judge Baumgartner called the attack “plainly dangerous” and warned that “commercial success does not attract preferential treatment” in court.

In sentencing, he said: “The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained.”
CCTV footage was shown in which Brown was seen striking Abraham Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head and then hitting his shoulder.

Heidi Stonecliffe KC, prosecuting, told the court Brown used a “heavy square-shaped tequila bottle” to “hit Mr Diaw twice over the left-hand side of his head”. He rained down “further blows” as Diaw turned away, the court heard.
Stonecliffe said Akinlolu then grabbed Diaw in a “bear hug”. She said: “Mr Diaw falls to the ground and Mr Brown is also seen throwing punches.”
In another clip, Brown, from California, could be seen being pulled away from the victim. The incident took place at about 3am and lasted about 20 seconds, the court heard.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died.
Emmy-award winning voice actor's family said he passed away 'suddenly' in an Instagram post
Eric Bauza of Scarborough, Ont., the Emmy-award winning voice actor best known for the iconic Bugs Bunny, has died. He was 46.
Bauza's family announced he had passed away "suddenly" in a post to his Instagram profile Sunday night. The family did not say the cause of death, but indicated they would share more at a later time.

Bauza grew up watching Bugs Bunny's exploits on the Looney Tunes cartoons at his home in the city. In 2020, he was charged with bringing the character to life in all his carrot-munching, prank-pulling glory.
"It is a dream come true," Bauza told host Ismaila Alfa on CBC Radio's Metro Morning at the time.

In addition to Bugs Bunny, Bauza voiced multiple other characters including Daffy Duck, Tweety Bird and Marvin the Martian. It took two auditions and plenty of practice to land the parts, he told Alfa.
In 2020, he gave his advice to young voice actors, telling them to remember that, at its base, it's "about the acting, first."
"You have to instill a performance that's grounded in reality," he said.
With files from CBC's Kate McGillivray

articles.title: 3 Negros groups unite vs ‘World Bank-DOTr scheme’ on transport modernization
articles.summary: Gerry Llena, LTFRB regional director for Negros Island, tells Rappler the allegation that three traditional jeepneys will be junked in exchange for one modernized unit is 'just a myth’

items: Three transport groups in Negros Occidental and Bacolod City, representing over 3,000 jeepney operators, are protesting against the World Bank and DOTr's Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP), fearing it will eliminate traditional jeepneys.

The PTMP aims to replace traditional jeepneys with modernized units, but operators are concerned about the financial burden and lack of feasibility studies, as well as the potential scrapping of their vehicles.
Transport leaders are calling for legal challenges against the program and seeking intervention from local officials, emphasizing their commitment to fight for their rights and livelihoods.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BACOLOD CITY, Philippines – Three transport groups in Negros Occidental and Bacolod City, representing over 3,000 traditional jeepney operators and drivers, have united against a joint scheme by the World Bank and the Department of Transportation (DOTr) that they say is poised to completely wipe them off the streets.

As they spoke up against the project, they intensified their protests at the start of a five-day Electric Vehicle Summit that kicked off at Ayala Malls Capitol Central in Bacolod on Monday, October 26.
On Thursday, October 22, they also staged a walkout at a World Bank–DOTr dialogue at Seda Hotel-Bacolod and held a surprise protest outside the hotel.
They condemned what they labeled as choreographed but nonsensical dialogue, designed just to please them into supporting the World Bank-DOTr transport modernization scheme.
These groups are:

items: Bacolod Alliance of Communters Operators and Drivers in Negros Island – Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkakaisang Termina ng Transportasyon (BACODNO-MANIBELA)
Kabakod Negros Transport Coalition (KNETCO)
United Drivers and Operators Center-Pinakaisang Samahan ng mga Tsuper at Operator Nationwide (UNDOC-PISTON)

blocks.text: Previously, they were known as fragmented transport groups in the province and its capital, Bacolod.
But faced with the proposed World Bank-DOTr Public Transport Modernization Program (PTMP), they were left with no alternative but to unite, or else they would be completely wiped off the streets.
PTMP is the rebranded version of the 9-year-old Public Utility Vehicle Modernization Program (PUVMP), which was originally implemented through DOTr Department Order No. 2017-011.

The PUVMP appears to be failing, having incurred a massive debt of approximately P5 billion with the Landbank of the Philippines (LBP) and Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) as the primary government lending institutions for the program.
Under the PUVMP, traditional jeepneys will be gradually phased out across the country and replaced by modernized units equipped with Euro 4-compliant engines.
Since each unit of a modernized jeepney costs more than P2 million, operators were required to form a cooperative before they could apply for a loan from the LBP or DBP.
In Negros Occidental, however, eight of the 11 transport cooperatives under the Bacolod Modernized Jeepney Transport Association (BMJTA) are facing significant issues.
A total of 329 units of modernized jeepneys belonging to the BMJTA are in danger of being repossessed by either the LBP or the DBP.

But under the PTMP, the World Bank is ready to extend loans—not to cooperatives, but to well-established transport companies and corporations with sterling performance records—to become the next operators of modernized jeepneys in the Philippines.
With PTMP, all modernized jeepneys will be upgraded from standard Euro 4 engines to Euro 4L-equipped units.
Under this scheme, three traditional jeepneys will be replaced with one unit of a Euro 4L-compliant modernized jeepney.

Once all hindrances are cleared, the DOTr will pilot the PTMP in five highly urbanized cities in the country, including Bacolod, Iloilo, Cebu, Baguio and General Santos, and in the National Capital Region (NCR).
In a press conference on Monday, October 26, Rudy Catedral, president of BACODNO-MANIBELA, however, said they are opposed to the program at all costs.
“It is the same intention, but this time, the DOTr is just masquerading as the World Bank to cover up its failed PUVMP,” Catedral emphasized. “PTMP will wipe us all out—it will ‘kill’ us all.”

blocks.caption: POWER. Women lead KNETCO protesters against the World Bank-DOTr’s new scheme on transport modernization program, on October 22, 2026. Photo by Ambo Delilan

blocks.text: For KNETCO president Lilian Sembrano, it is premature to fully roll out these modernized public utility vehicles—whether Euro 4L-compliant or fully electric (EV)—given the lack of guarantees regarding their capacity, reliability, and sustainability.

“But if the DOTr is really sincere about the PTMP, then they have to pilot it in areas without transport service entities (TSEs) for a year so we will know how effective the EVs to be funded by the World Bank are,” the KNETCO president said.
However, mixing those EVs with existing routes covered by TSEs will only complicate the situation, she added.
But Sembrano said their greatest fear is that under the PTMP, the DOTr will designate a scrapping center where traditional jeepneys will be hauled and demolished.
“Then, our traditional jeeps will be brought to a scrapping center? Gosh! What will happen to our treasured assets? Will they be junked, will they be shredded? Sakit naman (it hurts),” she added.
Sembrano stated that because the PUV Modernization Program is mandated only through a DOTr department order rather than a law, they intend to challenge it legally.
“We will fight for our rights. We will fight for our families,” she said.
Sembrano asked Bacolod Mayor Greg Gasataya to help them by intervening in the negotiation between the World Bank and the DOTr.

“Why force us to succumb to modernization when we cannot afford the P3 million to P4 million unit price of the modernized jeep to be financed by the World Bank?” Sembrano asked. “Can’t we focus on rehabilitation first?”
“Besides,” she added, “there’s no feasibility study presented to them about PTMP. So, are we ready for another mistake like the failed PUVMP?”
Rodolfo Gardoce, Jr., president of UNDOC-PISTON, said they will not hesitate to hold a massive “untat byahe” (stop the trip) at any time once the planned scheme of World Bank and DOTr pushes through.
Gerry Llena, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) regional director for Negros Island, told Rappler on Monday that he has yet to hear both sides of the issue.
“But the allegation that three traditional jeepneys will be junked in exchange for one modernized unit under the PTMP is just a myth,” he said.
“We are guided by the so-called Local Public Transport Route Plan (LPTRP), so we cannot just scrap jeepney units, or else we will face an even greater shortage,” he added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Peta releases video showing experiments on infant monkeys at University of Washington
articles.summary:
Animal-rights group released video footage that shows distressed baby macaques undergoing lab experiments

Footage released by the…

blocks.text: Footage released by the animal-rights group Peta reveals, for the first time, filmed experiments at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center (WaNPRC), in which newborn monkeys were separated from their mothers and subjected to neurological tests after prenatal exposure to a neurotoxin.

Records show that the infant monkeys, some just two days old, were used in research on domoic acid, a toxin produced by marine algae that accumulates in shellfish and can cause illness in humans. The experiments were part of a project that ran for six years until 2020.

The footage shows monkeys with electrodes attached to their heads, undergoing tests to investigate whether exposure to domoic acid in the womb had damaged their brains. The baby monkeys appear distressed as they clutch blankets, suck their fingers, screech, and jerk as experimenters shave their heads and test their reflexes and memory.

The infant macaques were bred at the University of Washington’s Infant Primate Research Laboratory for the project researching the developmental neurotoxicity of domoic acid in nonhuman primates. Researchers administered doses of domoic acid daily to 32 pregnant macaques. After birth, 28 infants were removed from their mothers, bottle-fed and kept in incubators before being housed individually at three weeks old.

“These monkeys are so young they still have the distinctive black fur of newborn macaques, yet instead of clinging to their mothers, they grasp blankets on metal tables,” says Peta’s chief science adviser on primate issues, Dr Lisa Jones-Engel.

blocks.caption: One of the project’s infant monkey experimental subjects. Photograph: Peta

blocks.text: In the wild, macaques live in close social groups. Infants have long-term maternal care needs for their social and behavioral development, says Dr Malene Hansen, a long-tailed macaque expert, and cannot thrive without their mothers. “It is unethical to conduct research that separates infant macaques from their mothers. Period,” she says.

The WaNBRC told the Guardian: “We recognize that research involving infant animals raises important questions about their wellbeing. Maternal relationships and early social development are important considerations in nonhuman primate welfare. Our experienced veterinary and animal care personnel have specialized expertise in primate care, including nursery rearing.”

The project ran from 2014 to 2020 and received more than $4.2m in National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding. Some experiments lasted years. According to Peta, the monkeys were killed after the experiments were concluded.

The NIH says it takes the care and use of laboratory animals very seriously: “All animals used in NIH-supported research are protected by laws, regulations and policies designed to ensure the smallest possible number of animals are used and their welfare is prioritized.”
According to the WaNBRC, there are no current infant studies at its center; however, protocols for such studies are active.

Jones-Engel says: “There is no moral escape hatch. You can’t claim primates are used because they’re so like us, then take an infant away from its mother and experiment on it. You would never do that to a human primate. The cruelty also has biological consequences: maternal separation alters an infant’s physiology, immunity, behavior and development, distorting its response to the very substance or disease being studied.”

Jones-Engel worked as a primate scientist at the University of Washington for 17 years and has spent 35 years working as a primatologist. Her transition from animal researcher to campaigner is documented in a new film, Sentient.

blocks.caption: One of the young monkeys from the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center. Photograph: Peta

blocks.text: Now one of the University of Washington’s most outspoken critics, Jones-Engel says the footage offers a rare glimpse into experiments involving monkeys: “For decades, the term ‘primate research’ has obscured the reality inside laboratories. These videos expose the suffering and raise a fundamental question: why are these facilities still operating at all?”
Peta is calling for the closure of all seven US National Primate Research Centers.

The footage relates to a research program that has operated at the University of Washington’s Infant Primate Research Laboratory since 1971 and emerges amid a long-running dispute between Peta and the university. In a 2020 lawsuit, Peta challenged the school’s handling of public-records requests. The court ruled that the university violated laws by failing to adequately search for records, in a case that revealed systematic destruction of photos and videos at the school.
The footage was released to Peta in September 2026 in response to a records request. The videos were filmed between 2017 and 2019.
The WaNPRC says the monkey studies have contributed to an understanding how prenatal domoic acid exposure may affect learning and memory: “These findings remain relevant to public health.”
However, there is no clear evidence that the experiments led to changes in public health recommendations.
Although the domoic acid research ended in 2020, records show that the WaNPRC continued to breed, purchase and use monkeys, including infants, to study viruses such as Epstein-Barr and HIV.

In a 2021 study, 25 infant rhesus macaques were infected with SIV, which is closely related to HIV. The study was looking at why some infants develop Aids more rapidly than others. The infected baby monkeys experienced significant distress, chronic diarrhea and body wasting, before they were killed for autopsy. In another study, 10 infant monkeys were separated from their mothers within two days of birth to test an experimental Epstein-Barr vaccine.

While supporters argue that biological similarities between humans and nonhuman primates make monkeys useful for studying human disease, decades of animal research has yet to produce an approved HIV vaccine.

Research scientist Dr Jarrod Bailey argues that biological differences mean monkey experiments often fail to deliver treatments for human diseases, including HIV/Aids, Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. “We pay the price in failed treatments; monkeys pay with their lives. A shift away from monkey experiments would benefit all primates – including humans.”

The University of Washington says it is committed to replacing, reducing, and refining animal experiments through emerging technologies and improved animal care, but says that “animal studies remain necessary for some complex scientific questions”.

In the US, federal agencies are shifting towards reducing animal testing in favor of new approach methodologies, including organ-on-a-chip technology and computer modeling. The NIH is also investing in human-based alternatives. Yet primate research remains widespread: more than 106,000 monkeys were held in US facilities in 2025, up 1.5% from 2024, and more than 32,000 primates were imported from Asia and Africa for laboratory use from 2025 to 2026.

articles.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] BIR backs down on QR badges. Will it dare audit the powerful?
articles.summary: Listening to taxpayers is good governance. But reversing a requirement five days before its deadline raises a bigger question.

blocks.text: An open letter to Commissioner Charlito Mendoza: Suspending the QR badge mandate is a welcome development. But the real test of tax reform is whether the BIR can investigate unexplained wealth without fear or favor.
Dear Commissioner Mendoza,
Your decision to suspend the mandatory display of BIR Registration Seal Badges under Revenue Memorandum Circular (RMC) No. 113-2026 deserves recognition.
The October 31 deadline has been suspended. Display is now voluntary, with no penalties solely for non-display during the suspension.

Listening to taxpayers is good governance. But reversing a requirement five days before its deadline raises a bigger question: Why weren’t privacy concerns, technical readiness, and stakeholder consultations addressed before compliance was required?

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) reported that more than 52,700 registration documents with badges had been secured by October 14. This warrants an assessment of taxpayers’ time and compliance costs.
The suspension should not mark the end of reform. It should establish a new standard for taxpayer-centered regulation.
Consider electronic invoicing or e-invoicing.

The TRAIN Law established a system-dependent framework beginning in 2018. Eight years later, RMC No. 98-2026 requires specified taxpayers to comply by December 31, with micro e-commerce taxpayers exempted. RMC No. 110-2026 introduces accreditation requirements for third-party service providers. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Guidelines on VAT for Nonresident Digital Service Providers)
I support digitalization. But if government needed eight years to implement reform, why should taxpayers shoulder disproportionate software costs, technical difficulties, and potential penalties?
Accreditation must safeguard data and promote competition—not create unnecessary barriers for Filipino technology providers.
GOVERNMENT DELAYS MUST NOT BECOME TAXPAYER PENALTIES.
Businesses struggling to comply are not automatically tax evaders. Modernization must make compliance easier for taxpayers—not merely administration easier for the BIR.
According to 2024 government statistics, MSMEs account for 99.63% of Philippine establishments and 66.58% of employment.
These enterprises deserve proportionate regulations, not unnecessary bureaucracy.
Meanwhile, the Philippines scored just 32 out of 100, ranking 120th among 182 countries, in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index.
The index does not establish wrongdoing by any individual. But it underscores a serious public-trust challenge.
One disturbing sentiment circulating online captures the frustration: “PAYING TAXES AT THIS POINT FEELS LIKE SPONSORING CRIMINALS.”
This is no justification for tax evasion. It is a warning about eroding confidence in government accountability.

Commissioner, I challenge the BIR to launch a NATIONWIDE, RISK-BASED TAX AUDIT INITIATIVE targeting credible evidence of undeclared taxable income and unexplained wealth involving politicians, political dynasties, and public officials—from barangay halls to Malacañang.
NO SACRED COWS.
NO POLITICAL EXEMPTIONS.
NO SELECTIVE ENFORCEMENT.
Wealth or political connections alone do not establish wrongdoing. But credible discrepancies between lawful income and accumulated assets deserve investigation.

Use legally authorized cross-checks of tax returns, Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), property records, and beneficial ownership information. Coordinate with the Ombudsman and the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) when warranted.
Build on RMO No. 22-2026 through three measurable reforms:

First, protect low-risk taxpayers. Generally exclude startups during their first three years and MSMEs with annual sales not exceeding ₱100 million from routine audit, except where credible tax risks exist.
Second, reduce compliance costs. Provide affordable electronic invoicing, just transition, and competitive provider accreditation.
Third, demonstrate accountability. Publish anonymized results on high-risk investigations, final assessments, actual collections, and taxpayer compliance costs.
Commissioner, suspending the badge requirement shows that the BIR can respond when taxpayers raise legitimate concerns.
But the bigger test is whether it can investigate the politically powerful with the same determination it regulates ordinary Filipinos.
CAN THE BIR AUDIT THE POWERFUL WITH THE SAME ZEAL IT AUDITS ORDINARY TAXPAYERS?
Because honest taxpayers are not the enemy. Corruption and tax evasion are.
AUDIT THE POWERFUL.
PROTECT THE SMALL.
RESTORE PUBLIC TRUST.

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal). He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.

blocks.text: Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".

articles.title: Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns
articles.summary:
Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”.

The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.

In its annual cyber threat report, ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire.
“We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday.
“Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.”

The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future.

ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”.

The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities, but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern.
The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses.
“To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said.

She has spoken previously about ASD having access to Anthropic’s Mythos model, the powerful AI tool which the frontier lab said it couldn’t release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity.
“To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release.
Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”.
after newsletter promotion

Bradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats.
Last week, newly discovered vulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language that underpins most websites – triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem.
ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents.
Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured.
“In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said.

articles.title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
articles.summary: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByBernd Debusmann Jr and Mike Hills
Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.
1. A border that is largely closed

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing the numbers detained at the southern US border since 2017. The red bars denote Trump's first term and his second term so far. The blue bars show Biden's term. The chart shows numbers peaked midway in Trump's first term at about 140,000 a month but came down again before starting…

blocks.text: To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
2. Building of wall speeding up
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

blocks.caption: Map showing where Trump has built a border wall between US and Mexico

blocks.text: "Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
3. Detentions and deportations rocketing

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

blocks.caption: Monthly bar chart of people detained by ICE for the first time between 2019 and 2026. Arrests were generally around 10,000 to 12,000 a month during Trump's first term before falling in 2020. Under Biden, arrests gradually rose from around 2,000 a month in early 2021 to about 8,000 by late 2024. A…

blocks.text: But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.
Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
4. Refugee intake down sharply
After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".
Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual refugee admissions to the US from 2017 to 2026. Admissions fell sharply during Donald Trump’s first term, dropping from about 53,000 in 2017 to around 12,000 in 2020. Under Joe Biden, admissions increased each year, reaching about 100,000 in 2024. After Trump returned to…

blocks.text: By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.
One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket
Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.
Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.
Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.

blocks.caption: Bar chart showing annual H-1B visa registrations from fiscal years 2021 to 2026. During the Biden administration, registrations rose from about 275,000 in 2021 to nearly 800,000 in 2024. Registrations then declined, with fiscal year 2025 at about 480,000 and fiscal year 2026 at around 360,000 aft…

blocks.text: Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.
The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.
At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.
