articles.title: Trump intensifies anti-Muslim rhetoric against Abdul El-Sayed at Michigan rally – US politics live
articles.summary: The US president was condemned for remarks that questioned the senate candidate’s loyalty to the country

blocks.text: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security.

The president also questioned his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally. Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

He also repeatedly invoked 9/11, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93, AP reported.
El-Sayed, who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country “shameful” and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups.

The Republican president’s remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president’s outreach to Arab American voters in 2024. “The president’s statements are out of line,” he said in a phone interview. “They are crossing a red line. They are racist.”

Trump also reiterated his apparent love for buxom bums and encouraged the crowd to compliment rapper Nicki Minaj’s behind. The comments about Minaj’s derriere came as he explained his recent observation on the Republican Ohio senator Jon Husted’s rear end.

Earlier in October, Trump said of the former college football player: “I don’t do this with men very often. I started examining his body, because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass and I looked at the whole – and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws.”
“You are a great athlete,” Trump also said to Husted. “Congratulations.” Trump was speaking at the rally to support Mike Rogers, the Michigan Republican Senate candidate.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision.

Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s attorney general, lashed out during an interview on Sunday while defending the justice department’s pre-emptive lawsuit to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate results if the GOP incumbent loses, calling a TV host’s question “crazy”. The testy repartee unfolded on CNN’s State of the Union over the DoJ’s unprecedented legal action, which alleges that there could be “voter confusion” due to two candidates named Dan Sullivan on Alaska’s ballot. Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it” when asked about the suit.

The US military has given Elon Musk’s SpaceX access to restricted space tracking data, raising a new round of questions about whether the Trump administration is attempting to hand over traffic control in Earth’s orbit to a controversial donor. articles.title: About 90,000 properties still without power after two storms strike Britain
articles.summary:
More strong winds are forecast after Storms Boelo and Austen cause travel disruption, flooding and kill two people

About 90,000 properties across northern parts of the UK are still without…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: About 90,000 properties across northern parts of the UK are still without power after a weekend of stormy weather, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come.
Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms, Austen and Boelo, pummelled parts of the UK, bringing widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations.
On Monday morning, the Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power.

The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend.
He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen.”

blocks.caption: Storm Boelo causes severe flooding in town centre of Largs, Scotland

blocks.text: Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northern Scotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc.”

The weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way and issued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times. The Met Office warned people to take care near cliffs and be aware of strong waves.

The second warning is in place from 3am to 9pm on Tuesday and covers most of Scotland. Forecasters said winds of 50-60mph were likely to be quite widespread with gusts up to 70mph in the far north. It warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and more power cuts.
The weekend storms led to two deaths, authorities said. A 60-year-old man was hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway while a man in his 20s died in Finchley, north London.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency teams and forecasters on Sunday to discuss the ongoing response to the weather, amid the warnings of more to come.

blocks.caption: A downed tree in Gladstone Park, London, on Sunday after strong winds overnight.  Photograph: Martin Evans/PA

blocks.text: On Monday, Swinney posted on X: “My deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the two people who have tragically lost their lives as a result of Storm Boelo. My thoughts are with all those affected by the damage and I thank the emergency services working through the night to keep people safe.”

There were also pockets of flooding with dramatic footage from Largs town centre showing flood water cascading through the town centre. One resident said it was the highest she had ever seen in 36 years of living there. Staff at the Thai restaurant Tha-Tien-Thai shared a video of their kitchen overrun by water with the desperate caption: “There is nothing left.” They said its doors would be closed for the foreseeable future “due to larger flood restoration than originally planned”.

Emergency services were called to a flooded care home in Saltcoats, North Ayrshire, on Sunday evening. Police Scotland said everyone at the care home was accounted for, road closures were in place and officers were expected to remain on site overnight to assist.

There was also travel disruption, with being flights diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford, England’s highest airport, and others cancelled. Most train services were getting back to normal although operators advised customers to check before they travelled.

The storms brought a number of event cancellations including the Sunday racing at Aintree, abandoned because of the high winds. The Guardian’s live blog of the tea-time Sunderland v Leeds goalless draw summed up the action: “And the winner is … the wind.”

articles.title: Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza dies at 46
articles.summary: Bauza was best known for voicing iconic 'Looney Tunes' characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-Canadian voice actor Eric Bauza, best known for voicing iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, died on Sunday, October 25. He was 46.
His family announced his death in a statement posted on Instagram on Sunday. They had referred to his passing as “sudden.”
View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝙀𝙍𝙄𝘾 𝘽𝘼𝙐𝙕𝘼 (@bauzilla)

Born in Scarborough, Ontario, Canada, on December 7, 1979, Bauza grew up watching Looney Tunes and imitating its characters.He later became one of the franchise’s defining modern voices following in the footsteps of legendary voice actor Mel Blanc.Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, and Road Runner, among other characters. He lent his voice to films like Space Jam: A New Legacy, Super Mario Bros., and King Tweeny.
His latest work before his passing was Coyote vs. Acme, which premiered in August 2026. He had voiced Wile E. Coyote in the Dave Green-directed comedy film.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza said the appeal of Looney Tunes crossed cultural and language barriers.“Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures,” he said. “It doesn’t matter what part of the planet you’re from. You get the comedy.”Beyond Looney Tunes, Bauza lent his voice to hundreds of projects across film, television, and video games, including The Adventures of Puss in Boots, Teen Titans Go!, Ben 10, and The Super Mario Bros. Movie. His career spanned more than 25 years, with over 400 acting credits.He won three Children’s and Family Emmy Awards between 2022 and 2025 for his voice performance.
@CoyoteACMEMovie pic.twitter.com/H992Ff6tSO— Eric Bauza (@bauzilla) August 24, 2026

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Television Group chair Channing Dungey paid tribute to Bauza, saying he brought “joy and laughter to millions around the world.”“He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc,” Dungey added, honoring Bauza’s 15 years with Warner Bros. animation. – Neo Croox/Rappler.com
Neo Croox is a Rappler intern taking up journalism at the University of Santo Tomas.

articles.title: Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US
articles.summary: Latest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics project

blocks.text: Anthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.

The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a $1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.

“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said, adding that it has since taken steps to block similar actions.

Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issues a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors, which resulted in it requesting a token and gaining access to the information.
The AI developer said it had since put in place guardrails to prevent similar actions happening again. The incident was first reported by the news website Axios.

Anthropic had pointed out the unauthorised behaviour earlier in the month, when it said in a blogpost it found examples of ​Claude “working around a restriction to reach data that ‌was ⁠gated by a token or a fee” and that some of these cases involved websites run by US ​government agencies. At the time, it said the incidents had “minimal real-world impact”.

The unintended actions flagged by Anthropic included a model submitting a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police department. The US state department also revealed this month that Anthropic model had filed 19 visa applications in August.

Examples of unauthorised behaviour by AI agents – programs powered by AI models that carry out tasks autonomously – have been mounting since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, revealed in July that its bots had hacked an AI startup.

Since then, it has emerged that an OpenAI agent hacked the Australian healthcare system and the UK’s AI security institute revealed that Anthropic agents had carried out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test.

This month, the UK’s AI minister said he expected an AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the Australia hack, describing such an incident as likely, “if not inevitable”. Kanishka Narayan said the government will consider using the cyber ecurity and resilience bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.

In the US, the White House’s newly formed Super Intelligence Force – a federal body overseeing AI development – is mandating that all AI companies report security incidents involving their technology.

articles.title: Lustre denied due process in cyberlibel case -- Fadullon
articles.summary: Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon on Monday said veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest…

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 7:02pm

Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon on Monday said veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest warrant was issued against him.

“Apparently, in this particular case, reliance was made on the information provided in the investigation data form saying that he was connected with Philippine Daily Inquirer. That’s why he never received his copy of the complaint,” Fadullon said in an ambush interview.

“That’s why I believe the respondent and the lawyer are claiming that they were not given due process. I would have to agree with them that they were not given due process, as they were not given the opportunity to answer,” he added.
GMA News Online reached out to the Office of the City Prosecutor in Davao City and will update this story once a response is received.
Police officers arrested Lustre in Quezon City on Saturday on the strength of a cyberlibel arrest warrant issued by a court in Davao City.

Lustre’s camp said it was looking into what appeared to be a violation of his right to due process during the preliminary investigation, as he had neither been served nor received a subpoena or notice.
Fadullon said Lustre could file a motion to reopen the preliminary investigation.

Earlier, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said the Department of Justice (DOJ) should investigate claims that Lustre was not served a subpoena. Remulla also alleged that there was a “modus” in which complainants provide incorrect addresses for respondents.

Under existing DOJ circulars, Fadullon said, the prosecutor should have exercised due diligence in verifying the information in the investigation data form, including the respondent’s address and employment details.
He said a proper evaluation would have established that Lustre was no longer connected with the Philippine Daily Inquirer (PDI).
“As I said, if there had been a proper evaluation and the evaluating prosecutor had exercised due diligence, they would have ascertained that this person was no longer connected with PDI,” he said.
Fadullon, however, said he did not believe the error was intentional.

He added that his office could not initiate an investigation into the matter, but Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida could order a motu proprio investigation, or one initiated on the department’s own initiative.
Meanwhile, Fadullon said the complainant could face a perjury charge if an investigation established that the wrong employment information was deliberately provided.

“If it turns out later in the investigation and evaluation that the complainant knew that he was never really connected with PDI but still made it appear that he was, that could become an issue,” he said.
“Remember that the investigation data form is under oath so ( complainant) can be held liable there for perjury,” he added.
Lustre has been temporarily released from detention after posting bail of P48,000.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño
articles.summary: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to…

blocks.text: The water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.
“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”

blocks.caption: Cayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.
“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”

Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.
The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.

The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital.

Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.

blocks.caption: An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.
Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.
“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.

When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country.  Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters

blocks.text: US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”
Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño.

Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”
Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.
“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.

US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.

blocks.caption: Arbey Abdi Famu, a resident of the Dalhiska displacement camp in Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.

Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.

His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.

blocks.caption: People on the streets of Kismayo, where long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.   Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.
The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.

Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.
“They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.

Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.

Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.
Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.
Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”

Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.
“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”
Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.

blocks.caption: A mother takes her baby to a Somalia Red Crescent Society health centre in Kismayo to check for symptoms of malnutrition.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes.
Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region.
Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.
David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”

blocks.caption: A malnourished three-month-old baby in Kismayo hospital’s intensive-care ward in September. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”
Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.

Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.
Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.
Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”
In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.

Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.
El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine.

Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.
Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.

blocks.caption: Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital.  Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

blocks.text: For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.
“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.

Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.

articles.title: ‘It’s a mess right now’: RFK’s sweeping changes place new vaccines in limbo
articles.summary:
Health secretary’s effort to alter makeup of ACIP panel means no new recommendations coming – even as new vaccines are approved

US vaccine recommendations are in limbo, access to vaccines is…

blocks.text: US vaccine recommendations are in limbo, access to vaccines is suffering, and some of the uncertainty may continue for years following major blows to vaccination by the Trump administration, experts say.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), has made sweeping changes to vaccination policy, cutting childhood immunization recommendations by a third and replacing experts on the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) with his own handpicked allies.

A judge’s order halted these changes because they were not done correctly, but Kennedy has not nominated any new ACIP members – which means there are no new vaccination recommendations coming from the committee, even as new vaccines are approved.

Ron Kroening, 63, has asthma and bad allergies this time of year, so his doctor recommended the new Moderna mRNA flu vaccine, approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August for ages 50 and up. Trials suggest it provides even stronger protection than traditional flu shots.
It took time to locate the one pharmacy in his area that stocked the shot – and then Kroening was shocked to be charged a $40 co-pay.

“I figured that was an error because I’ve never had to pay for a flu shot in my life,” he said. But his insurance company told him it’s because there’s no recommendation from the ACIP, Kroening said: “The reason the mRNA isn’t covered is because it’s not listed as an ACIP vaccine.”
If the ACIP doesn’t recommend the new shot by the end of the year – a scenario experts say is likely – insurers won’t be required to cover it until January 2029 at the earliest.

“This is really a barrier. And any barrier to immunizations is going to keep people from getting them,” said Kroening, a retired public health employee who worked on immunizations at the state level in Oklahoma. “A $40 co-pay is going to turn people off,” he added, noting that his pharmacist also didn’t inform him that there were other flu shot options.

Insurers usually have at least a year after FDA approval to add coverage of a new vaccine to their plans, so a co-pay like Kroening’s isn’t unusual in the first year or so. But the difference now is it’s not clear when the vaccine will be fully covered.

Typically, when a vaccine is approved for a new group of people – either because it’s new to the market or because the approval expanded to include more people – insurers have a year from the recommendation to implement it by the next plan year, which usually starts in January. That means if a vaccine is recommended by ACIP in December 2026, insurers are required to cover it by January 2028. If it’s recommended a month later, in January 2027, then the coverage requirement is pushed to January 2029.
“The legal requirement doesn’t go into effect very quickly. The process takes time,” said Lindsay Wiley, professor of law and faculty director of the Health Law and Policy Program at UCLA Law.

For the new flu shot, “it seems likely that at best we would get a recommendation next year,” Wiley said, “but there’s no reason to think” they will do so. “It’s just delaying more and more and more,” she said.

The only exception to the law on coverage is for Covid vaccines, because Congress amended the Affordable Care Act to specifically include coverage of Covid immunizations within 15 days of ACIP recommendation.

The uncertainty around ACIP has other ripple effects. Some states won’t allow pharmacists to give vaccines without an ACIP recommendation. Some of the decisions the committee made before it was disbanded were also halted, including the September 2025 recommendation on new shots to prevent RSV – though insurers appear to be covering them anyway. A now-voided vote to end the universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine is influencing potential state-level laws.
There have also been delays reported for insurers covering the new flu shots for seniors under Medicare, which is mandated by law even without an ACIP recommendation.

The US government has appealed the part of the judge’s order that disbanded the vaccines committee, but there’s nothing to stop Kennedy from undergoing the correct process for appointing new members, experts say. He hasn’t.

“This White House and DoJ are making no serious attempt to actually revive the vaccine committee,” Aaron Siri, who has served as Kennedy’s lawyer and has litigated cases against vaccine makers, wrote on Monday. Siri added: “It appears the DOJ and the White House are doing everything they can to make sure that there is no functioning vaccine committee.”
Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco, agreed.

“The federal government is choosing not to put in place a new ACIP,” she said. She also noted that Kennedy’s slate of advisers were clearly “uninformed” about vaccine policy and it was “embarrassing”, even for anti-vaccine activists, to watch the public meetings.

There are some advantages for Kennedy not to have a functioning ACIP, Reiss said. “Kennedy, in appointing his ACIP, wanted to change the schedule, and they haven’t been anywhere near as quick as he’d like them to be. So, going around ACIP is a plus,” she said. Delaying the reconstitution of the committee may allow him to make his own recommendations, she added.
Even after the lengthy court case concludes, the way forward for ACIP is shaky, because Kennedy has “aggressively undermined” trust in the independence of the committee, Reiss said.

“Without dramatic changes, it’s probably not coming back the way it was,” she said. “This has shown that ACIP is politically vulnerable, and I think if we want ACIP to go back to the way it was, we’re going to need a statute that gives it some protection.”

Ron Kroening’s insurer is a member of the insurance industry group AHIP, which vowed to continue covering all shots recommended as of September 2025. And insurers can decide to cover vaccines before they’re required to do so.

“Vaccines are more cost-effective than getting the flu,” Kroening said. He said he still would choose the new vaccine despite the co-pay. “I’m able to pay the $40, and I’m happy I did, but still not happy that insurance didn’t cover it,” he said.
He’s worried about what all of this means for the future of immunizations in America. “They’re harder to get now,” Kroening said. “It’s a mess right now, what they’re doing with our vaccines.”

articles.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
articles.summary:
Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran

European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears…

blocks.text: European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) per megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.
The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p per therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports that the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.
Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains over $114 (£85) a barrel.

Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.

Britain’s energy regulators have warned that the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores across the continent after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.
It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid.
after newsletter promotion
Meanwhile British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual billl.

European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

articles.title: Jordan arrests 3 suspects in deadly church attack, state media says
articles.summary: Jordanian security forces arrested three armed suspects after a shootout on Monday in connection with an attack on a church last week that killed nine people, state television reported.

image.caption: Sahar Al-Halsa, who survived Friday's shooting at the church, gestures toward it while recounting what she witnessed during the attack, as she speaks to Reuters at her home next to the church in Karak, Jordan. (Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
Jordanian security forces arrested three armed suspects after a shootout on Monday in connection with an attack on a church last week that killed nine people, state television reported.
Suspects were found hiding in abandoned house, authorities say

Jordanian security forces arrested three armed suspects after a shootout on Monday in connection with an attack on a church in the U.S.-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported.

Friday's attack during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, in Karak governorate, about 120 kilometres southwest of the capital of Amman, also wounded 40 others. Witnesses said the shooting lasted several minutes.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said the suspects were located while hiding in an abandoned house in Karak. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them, the directorate said in a statement published on state media.
No security personnel were injured, it said, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects' possession.

items: Jordan king orders 'iron fist' response amid search for suspects in deadly church attack

blocks.text: Jordanian authorities have said the violence was carried out by "extremist terrorists." There has been no claim of responsibility.
A building shows signs of gunfire at the site where Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects in connection with Friday's shooting. (Alaa Al Sukhni/Reuters)
"Terrorism has no place among us," the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their "just fate."
King Abdullah, a U.S. partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to the rare attack on the Christian minority.
Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.
The Public Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people toward extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.

articles.title: NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November, says BMA
articles.summary:
Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November, with only emergency cover provided, union says

Senior doctors in England plan to go on strike for two days in November, the…

blocks.text: Senior doctors in England plan to go on strike for two days in November, the British Medical Association has said.
The industrial action by consultants is to begin at 6.59am on 25 November, with only emergency cover to be provided.

More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. The strike could be avoided if Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, committed to formal negotiations on pay and working conditions, the BMA said. The doctors were given a 3.5% pay increase this year.

Consultants in England last went on strike in 2023 but have been in dispute with the government since last year. Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee, said: “As the most senior and skilled doctors in the NHS, consultants not only provide frontline, life-saving care, but they are central to running and designing services, training and supervising the future workforce, and ensuring patients get the best treatment possible.

“Solving the pressures facing the health service will be impossible without valuing and retaining these doctors. Yet the government is failing to recognise this, ignoring our concerns around consultants’ wellbeing and workload, and pushing them further away from the NHS.
“And as the much-lauded progress on waiting lists in England stalls, the government is also telling consultants they deserve another pay cut.

“Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions, but time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out and we have been forced to announce strikes.
“Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough.

“Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.

“The government has four weeks to avoid any action taking place. We look forward to hearing from the secretary of state on areas that we can work on together to prevent these strikes, end the dispute and restore the role of the consultant in the NHS so that patients can benefit from the best clinical leaders long into the future.”

articles.title: Bill filed establishing ecozone for Pax Silica ops, other critical industries
articles.summary: The House of Representatives has proposed establishing an Advanced Industries Zone in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, saying it will create jobs and attract investments, including those from the…

blocks.text: The House of Representatives has proposed establishing an Advanced Industries Zone in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac, saying it will create jobs and attract investments, including those from the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which involves developing artificial intelligence (AID) systems, critical minerals, and more.

The National Union Party (NUP), led by House Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno of Antipolo and Bataan Rep. Albert Garcia, made the proposal under House Bill 11758, or the Advanced Industries Development Act (AIDA).

The bill provides that the Advanced Industries Zone will serve as “the country's national platform for strategic technology, advanced manufacturing, and innovation, under a dedicated authority empowered to attract investment and deliver government services efficiently.”

In return for competitive incentives, the bill states that enterprises or locators in the Advanced Industries Zone must create jobs for Filipinos, train Filipino workers, and transfer skills and know-how, so that Filipinos will not only assemble these technologies but ultimately design, build, and manage them later on.

The lawmakers noted that although the Philippines joined the US-led Pax Silica coalition in April 2026 alongside more than 20 other countries to build secure and resilient supply chains for AI technologies, membership alone would not guarantee investments without a clear, institutionalized legal framework that ensures policy continuity beyond the terms of incumbent public officials.

“The 1987 Constitution commands the State to give priority to science and technology and to pursue the industrialization and full employment of the nation. Today, the global technology supply chain is being redrawn, and the decisions being made now will shape where factories, research centers, and high-paying jobs will be located for a generation. Membership in Pax Silica opens the door, but it does not guarantee that the investments will come to us,” the bill read.

“Investors of this magnitude do not commit on promises alone. They look for clear rules, efficient government, and the assurance that the terms they rely on will not change with every administration. Our communities, in turn, deserve the assurance that growth will respect their rights and benefit their families. Only a law passed by Congress can provide both,” the bill added.
The bill sets a minimum investment of P15 billion per locator or qualified enterprise, exclusive of the value of the land.
The AIDA will have the authority to adjust the foregoing amount to reflect the cumulative change in the Consumer Price Index as published by the Philippine Statistics Authority every five years.
Further, it states that no adjustment will reduce the amount below that first prescribed, and no adjustment will affect a project already registered.

An expansion of the registered project of a qualified enterprise involving an additional investment capital of at least P5 billion exclusive of the value of the land may also be registered as a separate registered project but will only be entitled to limited incentives.
A qualified enterprise shall be entitled to the following incentives:

items: income tax holiday for seven years from the start of commercial operations of the registered project, but not later than three years from the date of its Certificate of Registration

a qualified enterprise can avail of either the Special Corporate Income Tax (SCIT) or the Enhanced Deductions Regime for a period not exceeding 20 years upon expiration of the income tax holiday, provided that the aggregate period of availment under subsections will in no case exceed 20 years from the date of the Certificate of Registration of the registered project

special corporate income tax equivalent to 5 percent of a locator’s gross income earned from the registered project, instead of all national and local taxes, fees, and charges, except real property tax on land, provided, that customs duties and the value-added tax on importation, among others.

blocks.text: Goods brought into the Advance Industries Zone from a foreign country will be subject to customs duties, value-added tax, excise tax, or other national internal revenue taxes upon entry, and will not be deemed imported into the Philippines for so long as they remain within the Zone.

The bill allows such goods to be stored, warehoused, broken up, repacked, assembled, sorted, graded, cleaned, mixed with foreign or domestic goods, processed, manufactured, tested, refurbished, or otherwise manipulated within the Advance Industries Zone without the payment of duties and taxes, and may be exported directly from the Advance Industries Zone free of duties and taxes.
This treatment, however, will only cover goods admitted for storage, processing, manufacturing, testing, research, or use in the operations of a locator or qualified enterprise.

“This is the most meaningful piece of legislation that I think impacts the future of our country that resolves many of the doubts and problems that we face today. If we push this [for passage into law] with all the vigor that we have, we can look forward to a better generation of Filipinos who will live better and be happier,” Puno said.
Garcia said the Philippines has long had the potential of being a manufacturing hub since the first economic zone was established in Mariveles, Bataan in the 70s.
This resurgence, Garcia said, was not sustained due to a lack of permanent policy on such initiatives.

“A lot of big companies, global companies [were] located in Mariveles. There’s Ford, Mattel, which makes Barbie dolls, United Apparel, among others. It created thousands of jobs. In fact, it resulted in migration to Mariveles; that is why we have Ilocano, Bisaya community, even up to now, in Mariveles,” Garcia said.
Likewise, Puno and Camarines Sur Rep. Migz Villafuerte addressed the concerns raised by the indigenous people that the Pax Silica initiative will displace them from their ancestral domain.

“On the matter of the displaced original residents of those areas, we recognize that it's something we have to deal with properly. We recognize that it is a reality that cannot be avoided. And I'm pretty sure that it will get the attention that it deserves. We will stay away from those areas as best we can,” Puno said.
“Hindi tayo mangwawalanghiya ng tao rito,” Puno added. (We will not disrespect the people there.)
Villafuerte said the area of the Advanced Industries Zone will only cover the government’s patrimonial land.
“Only the areas of patrimonial land will be for lease. The ancestral land, those other areas in question, will be under negotiation,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

image.caption: Jordanian security forces arrested three suspects after a dawn shootoutImage: Alaa Al-Sukhni/REUTERS

blocks.text: State security forces in Jordan arrested three men on Monday morning in connection with a deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday, in which nine people were killed and around 40 more injured.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties as they recovered firearms and ammunition.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.
"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."
Middle East conflicts take toll on Jordan's tourism sector
Jordan: King Abdullah calls for 'iron first' response
King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.

articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] Yes, Marcos still shuffling his Cabinet
articles.summary: Ghosts from the past continue to haunt

blocks.text: Vince Dizon, pulled out from the transportation department a little more than a year ago to head the scandal-ridden Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), is back in his old gig as transportation czar, Malacañang announced on Monday, October 26. He swaps posts with the man who replaced him as transport secretary, Giovanni Lopez, now the new DPWH secretary.

Until his latest transfer, Dizon’s appointment as DPWH secretary had yet to be confirmed by the Commission on Appointments, and this showed in an awkward exchange between him and estranged presidential sister Senator Imee Marcos last month.

Dizon’s transfer also came on the heels of a spat with Senator Panfilo Lacson over the latter’s allegations that he seemed to be covering up for Senator Alan Peter Cayetano, who is being accused by Lacson of having anomalous flood control projects in Taguig. Dizon and Cayetano are longtime allies, having both served under the previous Duterte administration after playing key roles in the strongman’s successful 2016 presidential run.
Indeed, ghosts from the past continue to haunt.

On Saturday, October 24, we were disrupted by the news that a team of Quezon City cops, showing uncanny efficiency, arrested a 72-year-old veteran journalist while he was attending a media forum, over a warrant issued by a judge from Davao City, and in relation to an unknown case filed by an unknown complainant.

Philip Lustre Jr. is known to journalists of my generation as a savvy and prolific political reporter who did the rounds and made waves in his heyday, poking fun at power and unmasking its unholy alliances. For all his acerbic posts on social media especially against the Dutertes, he did not see this coming — a warrant bare in substance and brazen in form.

items: It broke the norm that journalists and newsrooms are used to: when they are charged with libel or cyber libel, they get notified of the complaint and have the right of reply.

Lustre said he was clueless about who filed a cyber libel complaint against him, and what about. That it reached the court meant it already passed the desk of a prosecutor who should have informed him about it.
The arrest warrant, dated October 2, came from Davao City Judge Retrina Fuentes, and this gives room for a reasonable assumption that this had something to do with the Dutertes.

Fuentes is the same judge who issued a warrant in 2022 against public intellectual and former vice presidential candidate Walden Bello, who was also arrested in Quezon City over two counts of cyber libel filed by a longtime aide of Vice President Sara Duterte, Jefry Tupas. Unlike Lustre, Bello knew that a prosecutor had indicted him and that an arrest would follow. He spent the night at a police headquarters and was released the following day after posting bail.

blocks.text: Lustre’s arrest came in the same week that Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo Duterte, a brother of the Vice President, filed a cyber libel complaint against executives and staff of media giant, GMA Network, over stories linking him and his sister to bribery. Included in the complaint were National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag and whistleblower Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. Read about Gracioso’s claims here.

Philippine journalists and media organizations have been pushing for the decriminalization of libel and, shortly after the cybercrime law was enacted in 2012, they have moved to declare it unconstitutional.

items: The High Court eventually declared the cybercrime law constitutional, but struck down some controversial provisions.
Still pending for justices to decide on, however, is a petition filed by Bello in 2023, that essentially asked the Tribunal to decriminalize libel.

blocks.text: The criminal aspect means that one who is charged with libel faces arrest and will be freed only after posting bail. To decriminalize libel does not absolve journalists of accountability; it simply turns it into a civil case that will still be litigated on top of the constant hurdles that powerful people in the Philippines throw at them — threats and harassment, reputational attacks, killings, bribery, closed access to information that the public needs to know.

The Philippines remains to be one of the most dangerous places for journalists globally, ranking 114th out of 180 countries and territories. “Despite its extremely dynamic media landscape, the Philippines is one of the most dangerous countries in the world for journalists,” according to the 2026 World Press Freedom Index.
Because in plain truth, beyond the reach of libel are those in power, who are already gifted with all means fair and foul for their so-called grievances.

items: Former president Rodrigo Duterte’s words, for instance, killed. And he’s proven it, as we wrote in this piece.

From 2012, when the cybercrime law was enacted, up to 2022, nearly 4,000 cases were filed in various agencies, with the national police saying that cyber libel makes up 20% of the crimes they investigate. Just imagine the other crimes that need more police attention.

Simply for practical reasons, decriminalizing libel “will free our public prosecutors to allocate their time… to prosecuting criminal cases that affect the national interest and our territorial integrity,” said lawyer Gilbert Andres in this story.

blocks.text: Speaking of territorial integrity: China’s agent-provocateur in Manila, Ambassador Jing Quan, also knows how to weaponize language, as we’ve seen in the past days as he fired volleys of criticism against Philippine officials.
How do we make sense of this gutter talk from the Chinese envoy? Bea Cupin weighs in in this piece.
But still a happy Monday to you! In a dramatic victory, Brazil President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva fended off a rally by far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, winning a historic fourth term.

articles.title: Manitoban denied out-of-province care for rare condition says he's 'tortured every single day'
articles.summary: A Manitoba man living with a rare genetic condition says he's now considering medically assisted dying, after being denied out-of-province coverage to get a procedure he and experts say he can't get…

image.caption: Manitoban Tomas Ponzilius has Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a rare genetic condition that affects connective tissues in the body. He's made two previous requests to get out-of-province treatment, but both were denied. (Alicia Wang/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A Manitoba man living with a rare genetic condition says he's now considering medically assisted dying, after being denied out-of-province coverage to get a procedure he and experts say he can't get here.
Tomas Ponzilius, who lives with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, says he's considered medically assisted death
Since he was a child, Tomas Ponzilius wanted to be a lawyer, a father and a disability rights advocate.
But these days, he spends most of his time in bed in his home in Winnipeg, before the chronic pain he lives with causes him to pass out, he says.
He's made two previous requests to get out-of-province treatment, but both were denied, leaving him considering exploring medically assisted dying.
"I don't want to die, but I'm being tortured every single day," the 33-year-old said. "This isn't a life."

Ponzilius has Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a rare genetic condition that affects connective tissues in the body. It makes the collagen in his body weaker and causes cervical instability, or instability at the part of the spine holding up the head.
Because of this, he experiences vision and breathing problems, along with extreme pain in his neck.
Ponzilius said he's run out of pain medication because he can't afford it and it's not covered by the province, and is cutting back on other treatments for the pain that cost $700 per month.
Ponzilius lives with vision and breathing problems, along with extreme pain in his neck due to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. (Alicia Wang/CBC)

He's asking Manitoba Health to approve his request to go to the U.S. for a cervical fusion, a surgical procedure that would stabilize his neck. It would cost about $200,000, but getting it would be "everything," he said.
He acknowledges the cost sounds high, but estimates the social supports he's forced to rely on because he's in too much pain to cost $50,000 per year.
"Our government might say, 'Well, we need to save money,'" he said. "Actually, your position is that we can cost our system."
'Left with no pathway'
In July, his neurosurgeon submitted a letter to the province's out-of-province referral program.

It states that the "rarity and complexity" of Ponzilius's condition means the required surgical expertise for the procedure, and the specialized rehabilitation services he'd need, are not available within Manitoba.
His request was rejected, with the province saying it needed more proof there wasn't sufficient care in Manitoba.
Ponzilius is currently waiting for Manitoba Health to decide on his appeal.
In the meantime, living with the disease makes it feel like "every single day I wake up, I roll a 20-sided die. I roll too low, I'm dead," Ponzilius said. "You can't wait with this."

items: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome forced a Winnipeg Jets draft pick to retire at 21. What is it?

blocks.text: CBC asked the health minister for a response on Ponzilius's case, but a spokesperson said the province can't comment while it's before the appeals board.

Though Ponzilius was born with Ehlers-Danlos, he was only diagnosed last year, by an American doctor. For most of his life, doctors here couldn't explain his dislocating shoulders and chronic pain, he said.
I wanted a childhood.… I wanted my 20s. I could still save my 30s.Tomas Ponzilius
He's had several procedures done in Manitoba in an attempt to stabilize his shoulders. The results were meant to last years, but the first lasted five months, the second just two or three weeks.
"It is not that we don't have excellent care in Manitoba, but this is a service gap," Ponzilius said. "We just don't have capacity, frankly, in Manitoba and we're left with no pathway."
Referred to U.S. clinic

Ponzilius was first rejected for out-of-province care last year, when he was referred to see Jan Dommerholt, who owns a Maryland clinic recognized by the non-profit Ehlers-Danlos Society for providing specialized care.
Instead, Manitoba Health told him to go to the GoodHope Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Clinic in Ontario, one of a few clinics in Canada that specializes in the condition.

In a statement emailed to CBC in response to questions about Ehlers-Danlos in Manitoba, a provincial spokesperson said "established referral pathways are available" to clinics in Canada if Manitoba lacks the specialized care a patient might need.
But the Ontario clinic told Ponzilius it isn't accepting out-of-province patients.

items: Manitoba partially repays retiree for out-of-country surgery after twice refusing to pick up the tab

blocks.text: Ponzilius says Manitoba Health should've known that. The same information came up in a separate application for out-of-province coverage from a woman with Ehlers-Danlos he spoke with when she applied. She successfully appealed the province's initial denial of out-of-province care in 2024.
Ponzilius paid for his visit to the Maryland clinic out of pocket.

Jan Dommerholt owns Bethesda Physiocare, which provides specialized Ehlers-Danlos syndrome care. He says he doesn't know of any surgeons in Canada who are qualified to perform the procedure Ponzilius would need. (Submitted by Jan Dommerholt)
Dommerholt said when he saw Ponzilius, he recommended he see a Maryland neurosurgeon who specializes in Ehlers-Danlos to perform the cervical fusion.
That procedure can normally be done by any neurosurgeon, but Ehlers-Danlos can make the tissues of the body far weaker.
"If the surgeon goes in and tries to fix things and there's nothing to even do stitches in because the tissues are too loose … what are you going to do?" said Dommerholt.
In its statement, the province said there are neurosurgeons in Manitoba who are trained to "assess and manage complex spinal conditions," including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Ponzilius has sent multiple letters to the minister of health asking who those people are, but hasn't got a response.
Dommerholt said only a handful surgeons worldwide are qualified, and none are in Canada.
Lost faith in system
That's also what the non-profit EDS Canada Foundation says.
Tammy Stadt, the foundation's resources director, says the province's request for more proof that Ponzilius can't get the care he needs in Manitoba places an unfair burden on him.
"Exhausting other access to care in Canada is very challenging, because a lot of specialists will not take referrals from other provinces," she said.
In denying his request, Manitoba Health told Ponzilius he hadn't proven the care he needs is "not adequately available in Manitoba or elsewhere in Canada."
But Stadt said while a procedure may be performed in-province, that doesn't mean it's being done with the right expertise.
In the meantime, Ponzilius is waiting for Manitoba Health to decide on his appeal. He thinks it will succeed, citing the 2024 precedent, but says he's lost faith in the system.
If he'd had the right interventions, he feels his life could have been different.
"I wanted a childhood... I wanted my 20s," he said.
"I could still save my 30s."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alicia Wang is a multimedia journalist with an interest in technology, disability and accessibility reporting. She has previously worked at Imprint and the Toronto Star and was a 2026 CBC News summer scholar.

Merz and Steinmeier head to Asia on separate trips
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are departing on separate Asian tours to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties.

Merz will visit Singapore, Japan and South Korea on his longest overseas trip since taking office, accompanied by a high-level business delegation. He is seeking to broaden Germany's partnerships and reduce dependence on individual countries.

In Singapore, he will hold political talks and deliver a major foreign policy speech before traveling to Japan. In South Korea, he will attend an Asia-Pacific business conference and visit the demilitarized zone separating North and South Korea.
Steinmeier will make his second state visit to China, pressing for fairer trade relations and action to address economic imbalances, according to his office.
He is expected to speak at Peking University on Thursday and meet President Xi Jinping and Premier Li Qiang on Friday.
Steinmeier also wants China to take greater international responsibility, including using its close ties with Moscow to help end Russia's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states
articles.summary:
Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army

Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five…

blocks.text: Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.

The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref, and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.
All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.
Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.
“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he was scared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled.
“We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.
Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.
Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.
Africa’s third-largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.
The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.

Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said over the phone from Al-Jazira’s Al-Junaid town: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.
“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.
Farmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.
Further east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”.
“Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss.”
Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and a currency that lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.

articles.title: NBI seeks transfer of Paolo Duterte's cyber libel complaint from Davao City
articles.summary: NBI Director Melvin Matibag said he will ask Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida for the transfer of the venue of the complaint from Davao to the DOJ-National Prosecution Service.

blocks.text: Published October 26, 2026 5:54pm

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag on Monday said he will file a motion to have the Davao City prosecutor’s office inhibited from handling the libel and cyber libel complaints filed by Davao Representative Paolo Duterte.
Matibag said he will also ask Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida for the transfer of the venue of the complaint from Davao to the DOJ-National Prosecution Service.
“For what reason? We found out that the City Prosecutor, Prosecutor [Jhopee] Avanceña, is [the] first cousin of Ms. Honeylet Avanceña,” he said in a briefing.
Honeylet Avanceña is the partner of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the congressman's fafther.

“Alam naman natin sabihin walang legal relationship because by affinity wala naman, dahil hindi naman kasal, but still it develops a sense of alarming reason for us to transfer dahil nandodoon pa rin ‘yung malalim na relationship. To remove the bias,” he added.

(We know that we can say there is no legal relationship by affinity because they [Rodrigo Duterte and Honeylet Avanceña] are not married, but it still gives us cause for concern and a reason to transfer because that deep relationship is still there. To remove the bias.)
Last week, Congressman Duterte filed a libel and cyberlibel complaint against Matibag, dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., and GMA Network executives and journalists.

This stemmed from Gracioso’s allegation that he delivered suitcases containing cash to Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte, and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instruction of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
They have denied the allegations.
Matibag said Vida may also appoint a special prosecutor for the complaint.
“It’s the discretion of the Secretary of Justice, probably can appoint a special prosecutor for this purpose,” he said.
Sought for comment, Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon said this is up to the Justice Secretary’s discretion.

“It really depends on what the grounds are that are being relied on for the transfer kasi we do not see any reason why the other offices of the department where the office, which has jurisdiction… cannot take cognizance of the case,” he said.

“They will have to provide us with justifications as to why it cannot be heard there or why it’s not feasible to conduct the hearing there before it can be transferred here and that is a matter that the secretary of justice will have to act on,” he added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
articles.summary:
Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’

Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or…

blocks.text: Chinese young adults looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having pets or children have found an answer: raising bricks.

Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.

Raising “brick babies” is easier than house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day and waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article praised the bricks as being “practically immortal”: “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform.

blocks.caption: Social media user documents their brick’s changes over a year, with hashtags including  #healingand #stress relief. Photograph: @South / xiaohongshu.com

blocks.text: Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick parent told Chinese media that the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.

One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick baby, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.”

“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”

Chinese young people are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society such as having children and grinding out long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the employment rate much higher.

China’s birthrate is in stubborn decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of studying in an intensely competitive educational environment, many young people are choosing to drop out of the rat race, and opting instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low effort, low stress lifestyle, well-suited to raising bricks.
The trend of raising bricks has become so popular that Chinese media has started to warn about the health risks.

Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of suffering from itchy eyes and a runny nose. Xuedong Li, a retired moss professor from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged brick parents to raise their mossy babies in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.
Additional research by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Mans Carpio is complainant behind journalist's 'irregular' arrest, says lawyer
articles.summary: The case stems from a March 6 Facebook post questioning whether Carpio helped fund the operation of the so-called “18 Marines.”

blocks.text: October 26, 2026 | 5:35pm
Composite image shows Mans Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, on April 27, 2026 and veteran journalist Philip Lustre upon his arrest in Quezon City on Oct. 24, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, filed the online libel complaint against veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. which led to his arrest over the weekend.
This is according to Lustre's lawyer, Dino de Leon, who shared a copy of the first page of the information sheet that was filed with the Davao City regional trial court on Monday, October 26.
"We have obtained the document. Mans Carpio, the husband of Sara Duterte, filed a complaint against veteran journalist Philip Lustre," De Leon wrote in a Facebook post in mixed English and Filipino.
The information sheet shows Lustre had been accused of online libel under Section 4(c)(4) of Republic Act 10175 or the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.
The offensive material in question was a March 6, 2026 Facebook post in which Lustre accused Carpio of being one of many supposed funders of the 18 self-claimed former bagmen.

These individuals, who now face a multitude of lawsuits over their allegations, claim to be former Marines who were contracted to deliver some P805 billion in kickbacks from flood control works to various officials, including the president.
The Philippine Navy has since clarified that four of the 18 were never Marines and most were dishonorably discharged.
De Leon agreed to become Lustre's lawyer on the spot as the arrest was carried out at a media forum they were both attending Saturday, October 24.
The lawyer has since flagged several irregularities in the arrest of Lustre reminiscent of the legal harassment that Duterte critics faced under former President Rodrigo Duterte.
